choices: Impossible to compare, since the two expressions are mathematically different

questions.q: The 'planning fallacy' describes a well-documented bias in time estimates. Even when a team knows that past similar projects ran over schedule, a project estimated to take 3 months will, on average, actually:
choices: Take longer than 3 months to complete
Take less than 3 months, since teams pad estimates generously
Vary randomly with no systematic tendency either way
Take almost exactly 3 months, since teams correct for known biases

questions.q: When people are asked to give a range they believe has a 98% chance of containing the true length of the Amazon River (a '98% confidence interval'), extensive calibration studies find that the true value falls outside most people's stated range far more often than 2% of the time — typically 30-40% of the time. What does this demonstrate?
choices: People are systematically overconfident: their stated intervals are far narrower than their claimed confidence level would require
People are well-calibrated: a 30-40% miss rate is expected for a 98% interval
The result just reflects random measurement noise, with no systematic bias
People are underconfident: their intervals are unnecessarily wide

questions.q: A golf coach notices that golfers who scored far above their personal average in Round 1 tend to score much closer to their normal average in Round 2, with no change in coaching between rounds. The coach concludes that his between-round pep talk caused this improvement. What statistical phenomenon better explains the shift, requiring no coaching effect at all?
choices: Simpson's paradox — the trend reverses once the data is split into subgroups
The hot-hand fallacy — made shots increase the odds of future makes
Regression to the mean — an unusually extreme score is partly due to luck, which doesn't repeat, so the next measurement drifts back toward the player's true average
Survivorship bias — only the golfers who kept playing are being observed

Removing one grain of sand from a heap never turns it into a 'non-heap' — one grain can't matter. Repeating this one grain at a time eventually removes the whole heap, yet each step seemed valid. What does this ancient puzzle (the Sorites paradox) actually demonstrate?
choices: That heaps do not really exist as objects.
That the correct definition of a heap is exactly 10,000 grains.
That mathematical induction is invalid for physical objects.
That vague predicates like 'heap' have no sharp boundary, so a chain of individually plausible small steps can lead to an absurd conclusion.
